item.title: US administrations asked Musk to switch Starlink on or off in multiple countries: Report
item.description: Biden and Trump governments sought SpaceX's help for internet access in Iran and military communications in Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: The administrations of former US President Joe Biden and current President Donald Trump have repeatedly asked Elon Musk's SpaceX to activate or restrict its Starlink satellite internet service in different countries, highlighting Washington's growing reliance on private technology companies to implement foreign policy objectives, according to a Reuters report citing six former senior US officials.The requests, made before the recent restrictions on Ukraine's military access to SpaceX satellite communications, included disabling Starlink to prevent Iran-backed militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using the service and activating it to provide internet access in Iran and Ukraine, Reuters reported.During Biden's presidency, US officials sought to restrict the service's availability to certain militant groups while also requesting its activation to support internet access in Iran and military communications in Ukraine, four former officials told Reuters.The Trump administration similarly asked Musk, SpaceX's chief executive, tomake Starlink available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026. The objective was to strengthen internet connectivity and communications for anti-government protesters, the report said.Ukraine restrictions raise questions over US-Musk tiesThe recent restrictions on Ukraine's access to SpaceX satellite services have renewed concerns about the relationship between the US government and Musk, whose company operates satellite communication systems considered important to the US military and its allies.The earlier requests by both administrations illustrate how Washington has increasingly depended on a private company to support diplomatic, political and military objectives abroad.The restrictions affecting Ukraine have also caused concern among European officials, some of whom argue that Europe needs to develop independent military satellite communication capabilities.European governments face a significant challenge because there is currently no readily available alternative that can immediately match SpaceX's capabilities, according to the report.Zelenskiy says restrictions affected military dronesUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that access to Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused satellite communication system, had been deliberately restricted, affecting the performance of Ukrainian military drones.He also said that Starlink connection speeds had been reduced. Ukraine relies on the service for several military operations, including frontline communications and defence against Russian missile attacks.Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).”Reuters previously reported that the order to restrict Starshield's operations in Ukraine originated within the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not confirmed whether it issued the order.The developments have raised questions about the extent to which a private technology provider can influence the communications capabilities of a country engaged in a war.Starlink remains critical to Ukraine's battlefield operationsStarlink has become a vital communication network for Ukrainian forces, connecting military units operating along the frontline. Ukrainian personnel have said there is currently no rival offering comparable capabilities.The service has helped maintain communications in areas where conventional networks have been damaged or disrupted by fighting.Starshield receivers, designed for military applications, are also used in Ukrainian drones as guidance systems and to maintain communication links with remote pilots. These systems support drone operations, including missions deep behind Russian lines within Ukraine. Their resistance to radio-frequency jamming has made them particularly valuable in a battlefield environment where electronic warfare is widespread.Europe considers alternatives to private satellite networksThe latest developments have intensified debate over the strategic risks of relying on privately owned satellite infrastructure for national security and military operations.For Ukraine, any disruption to satellite connectivity could affect coordination between military units and the operation of drones. For European governments, the episode has underscored the need to strengthen independent defence communications infrastructure.The repeated requests by successive US administrations also demonstrate how satellite internet services have become instruments of international policy, with decisions by a private company potentially carrying consequences for governments, armed forces and civilian populations.

item.title: Pakistan's LPG crisis deepens as prices hit 600 PKR/kg, hundreds of trucks stranded at Iran border
item.description: Pakistan's LPG imports from Iran have halted after two key border crossings were closed, pushing up cylinder prices and raising fears of worsening shortages. Traders warn of further increases as hundreds of trucks remain stranded and both countries discuss resuming trade.
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Jha
item.content:encoded: Pakistan is facing liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) shortages and rising prices after the closure of two border crossings with Iran disrupted supplies, Reuters reported.The Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings were shut on October 17, with the two countries offering different explanations. Pakistan's Balochistan government cited security concerns and efforts to curb smuggling, while Iran's foreign ministry attributed the closure to technical issues.Pakistan imports around 7,000 metric tonnes of LPG daily from Iran, according to the Pakistan LPG Association. More than 4,000 tonnes of the daily supply passes through Gabd-Rimdan alone, said Shamsul Haq, former president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry."These imports are at halt," Haq told Reuters.The disruption has pushed up LPG prices within days. Traders said the price of a 12-kg cylinder had climbed to 7,000 Pakistani rupees ($25) from 4,500 rupees ($16), with further increases possible if supplies remain disrupted.LPG prices rise across PakistanThe impact of the supply disruption is already being felt across the country. Pakistan LPG Association Chairman Irfan Khokhar told Reuters that a 12-kg cylinder was selling for around 7,000 rupees in Balochistan, 7,500 rupees in Lahore and 8,200 rupees in Skardu.Khokhar warned that shortages and price increases could intensify. He also said higher LPG prices were contributing to increases in the cost of other goods.Farhat Abbas, a resident of Lahore, told Reuters that the price he paid for LPG had doubled or more since the crossings were closed. He previously paid 250 rupees per kg but was now paying between 500 and 600 rupees per kg.Consumers are concerned that the supply constraints could worsen as winter approaches, when demand for fuel may rise.Trucks stranded as trade comes under pressureThe border closures have also disrupted the movement of goods between the two countries. Haq said hundreds of trucks, including LPG tankers, were stranded on both sides of the border.More than 1,000 Pakistani containers carrying potatoes, bananas and rice destined for Iran were also held up, he said. The Gabd-Rimdan crossing reopened on Wednesday for Pakistani exports of perishable goods, although LPG imports remained halted, according to the report.The Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry has advised its members to suspend new orders from Iran until further notice.Truck drivers stranded at the crossings described waiting for days in difficult conditions, with limited access to basic amenities. One driver, Abdul Ghani Baloch, told Reuters he had been waiting for more than a week for the border to reopen.Pakistan and Iran discuss resuming tradeThe disruption comes as Pakistan and Iran maintain significant cross-border trade ties. Bilateral trade stood at around $2.8 billion in the 2023-24 fiscal year, including approximately $684 million in Pakistani exports, according to the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry.Pakistan's army chief visited Tehran this week to discuss the US-Iran war and also held discussions with Iranian leaders on border issues. Iran's foreign ministry said consultations on restarting trade were under way.
